source: Simon & Chase (1973) Skill in Chess (American Scientist): de Groot's puzzle
finding: De Groot found that search statistics (moves examined, depth, speed) did not separate grandmasters from ordinary players. What separated them was memory for positions. This is the root of the pattern-recognition view of search.
numbers: Memory for 25-piece master-game positions: grandmasters and masters about 93% correct, experts about 72%, Class A about half, novices about 8 pieces (33%).
limits: Overview article, not a new experiment. de Groot's subjects were few and his search statistics were coarse.
agent_relevance: Skill on a search task may sit in what is noticed at the first look, not in how much is searched.

source: Simon & Chase (1973) Skill in Chess: eye movements and the MATER/PERCEIVER programs
finding: Tichomirov and Poznyanskaya recorded eye movements in the first 5 seconds of a best-move task. The pattern fits perception of chess relations (attack, defence), not a walk through a move tree. The PERCEIVER program simulated it.
numbers: About 20 fixations in 5 s. Most were on occupied squares. Many saccades went from a piece to a piece it attacked or defended.
limits: One expert subject in the Russian study. Eye movements show early perception only, not later search.
agent_relevance: The first seconds of a hard problem are a recognition phase. A scaffold can treat the first pass as cue reading before any branching.

source: Simon & Chase (1973) Skill in Chess: patterns trigger the move search
finding: Statement of the theory: patterns on the board are tied to plausible moves and trigger heuristics that start the move search. Masters notice good moves at a glance, then analyse for minutes, sometimes to find the first impulse wrong.
numbers: Chunk estimate of 50,000 patterns (P^7 > N argument, about 8x10^32 positions for P=50,000). Tournament time per move averages 3 to 4 minutes, up to half an hour on some moves.
quote: The pattern of an open file will trigger the heuristic and initiate a move in the heuristic search.
limits: The 50,000 figure is a crude extrapolation by their own words. The chunk prediction held only in part: the master recalled about twice the pieces of a Class A player, but chunks were only about 50% larger and the number of chunks was about 50% higher (first chunk 3.8 vs 2.6; chunks per position 7.7 vs 5.7).
agent_relevance: Cue then candidate then check is the S0 shape: recognise, propose, verify. The open-file rule means consider a Rook move, not play it.

source: Simon & Chase (1973) Skill in Chess: stored solutions and simultaneous play
finding: Masters beat weaker players in simultaneous play with a few seconds per move. The authors explain this by patterns linked to moves, and some patterns linked to whole solutions (traps, combinations).
numbers: Perhaps many hundreds of patterns carry an algorithmic solution (their estimate, no data).
limits: Informal observation from chess circles at the time, not measured.
agent_relevance: A fast path can rest on stored recognise-and-solve routines. The agent could keep a small library of such cases.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) The roles of recognition processes and look-ahead search in time-constrained expert problem solving (Psychological Science 7, 52-55): Kasparov simultaneous play
finding: Natural experiment: Kasparov (about 2750) played simultaneous games against national teams and a strong Hamburg team with one quarter to one eighth of the normal time per move. His estimated performance fell only about 100 Elo points.
numbers: Four to eight opponents, almost all masters or grandmasters. Worked Elo example: 2450 + 400(4.5-1.5)/6 = 2650 vs about 2750 in tournaments. No correlation between number of boards (hence speed) and his estimated performance.
quote: recognition, based on superior chess knowledge, plays a much larger part in high-level skill in this task than does planning by looking ahead
limits: Kasparov studied about 100 games of each opponent beforehand and steered into unfavourable positions, so preparation also cut search. One player. The match table was not in the text copy read. Opponents had full time.
agent_relevance: Strong play survives a large cut in thinking time when knowledge is rich. Supports a recognition gate before spending tokens.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Roles of recognition and look-ahead: search statistics and the de Groot replication
finding: De Groot: even grandmasters seldom look at more than 100 continuations. Gobet (1994) replication: masters did not differ from somewhat weaker players in maximum depth, but searched deeper on average than weak amateurs.
numbers: About 35 legal moves, so 35^6 = 1.8 billion lines three moves deep for each side. A master might examine 100 branches in 15 min (about 9 s per branch). Depth gain about 0.5 half-move per 200 Elo points (Charness 1981b; Holding & Reynolds 1982).
limits: The Gobet 1994 replication is an unpublished manuscript. Positions differed across studies. Charness proposes search becomes uniform at high skill.
agent_relevance: Search volume is small and nearly flat across skill. Good selection, not more search, is what scales. Matches our rule of checking a few candidates, not wide trees.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Roles of recognition and look-ahead: Holding's rival view and blitz data
finding: Holding (1985) argued that skill comes mainly from search and evaluation, not pattern recognition. Calderwood, Klein and Crandall (1988) found no big drop in move quality, rated by a grandmaster, between regular play and blitz.
numbers: Regular play 2.25 min per move vs blitz 5 min per game (about 6 s per move).
limits: Calderwood's ratings were subjective, which is why Gobet and Simon sought an Elo-based natural experiment.
agent_relevance: Competing view to keep in mind: recognition-only accounts may under-rate search on hard tactical positions.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: revisiting the chunking hypothesis (Memory 6, 225-255): recognition applied recursively in search
finding: Clearest statement of how recognition shortens search. After a move is made in the mind's eye, the new position goes back through pattern perception and new patterns suggest new moves. Holding wrongly read the theory as recognition only at the root.
numbers: Holding & Reynolds (1982): skill (1000 to 2200 Elo) did not correlate with recall of random positions but did correlate with the quality of search for the best move in them.
quote: pattern recognition is applied recursively during look-ahead
limits: The rebuttal (a memory test on the root position does not test recognition at later nodes) is a theory-saving argument, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Recognition should run at each node, not once. An S0-style cue check could be repeatable inside the search.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: templates and Holding's SEEK model
finding: Templates (large chunks) also give the class of the position, heuristics, plans and partial evaluation. Holding's SEEK model (Search, Evaluation, Knowledge) lacks a mechanism for how knowledge is retrieved. Pattern recognition would supply it.
numbers: Slots fill in about 1 s in the model; new chunks are learned at 5 to 10 s each.
limits: Slot-fill times are model assumptions, not measured in chess.
agent_relevance: A scaffold cue should return a plan and a check, not a bare answer.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: replication of the Chase and Simon copy and recall task
finding: Replication of the 1973 chunk method with more players and a computer mouse. The 2-second gap between placements still marks chunk boundaries. Masters used larger chunks than the 1973 master, who was inactive in chess.
numbers: 79.5% of within-chunk latencies were under 2 s vs 1.11% of between-chunk latencies; 89.3% vs 4.4% under 2.5 s. 74.6% of pieces in a chunk shared 3 or more relations vs 67.6% in Chase and Simon.
limits: Chase and Simon had one master, one expert and one Class A player. Mouse movement time had to be corrected. Larger master chunks than 1973 was not predicted by the original theory.
agent_relevance: The chunk is a measurable unit. Supports building a cue library from small groups of related items.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards (Cognitive Psychology 31, 1-40): experiment 1
finding: Masters, experts and Class A players saw 1 to 5 positions at 5 s each and recalled all. Percent recalled fell as boards were added, but masters kept far more than 7 chunks could hold. Hence templates in long-term memory, not only chunks in short-term memory.
numbers: N=13 (3 masters mean Elo 2453, 4 experts 2180, 6 Class A 1883). 26 positions of about 25 pieces. Masters placed up to about 60 pieces, experts about 40, Class A no more than about 20. Random positions: masters 21%, experts 16%, Class A 12% (F(2,10)=3.46, ns).
limits: Small N. The grandmaster lost a 5-board trial to an intrusion; without it masters at 5 boards = 50%. Serial position curve was U-shaped.
agent_relevance: Memory for a whole situation can be fast and large when a template exists. The agent may store one template per task type.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: experiments 2 and 3
finding: Longer gaps between boards helped recall, which fits encoding into long-term memory. A trained Chessmaster raised the number of boards he could reproduce above 70% average accuracy to nine over about 150 sessions, with up to 178 pieces correct.
numbers: Exp 2: gain from 1 s to 10 s gap was 71% (two boards) and 63% (four boards) for masters, 40% and 33% for experts. Four boards at 10 s gap: masters 82.9 pieces of 100, experts 44.9. Exp 3: session 89 = 9 boards, 163 pieces; session 130 = 9 boards, 167; session 150 = 9 boards, 178; one attempt at 10 boards, 160 pieces.
limits: Exp 3 is one subject. Boards above criterion stayed within the usual STM span. Cooke et al. (1993) found about 7 of 9 boards retained.
agent_relevance: Capacity limits can be passed by pointers into stored structures. For an LLM, retrieval of a stored template is the analogue.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: the template theory itself
finding: A template is a core pattern fixing perhaps a dozen pieces, plus slots for extra pieces, squares, openings, plans and moves, and links to other templates. Recognition needs only an EPAM-style discrimination net. Slots fill in under 1 s in the proposal.
numbers: Upper bound from Saariluoma (1989): masters retained a random position dictated at one piece every 2 s with 60% recall, so slots fill at 2 s or less with at least 60% accuracy. Predicts no more than 7 plus or minus 2 positions held.
quote: the raison d'etre for chessplayers' templates is to allow them to search efficiently while choosing a move
limits: No direct estimate of slot-fill time in chess. The paper says the purpose of templates is efficient search, but it does not test search itself.
agent_relevance: Template with slots is a good schema object: fixed core, variable slots, links to next templates.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: earlier challenges to chunking in short-term memory
finding: Anomalies for the pure STM chunking account. Charness (1976): a 30 s interfering delay cut recall only 6 to 8%. Bradley et al. (1987): visuospatial or central executive interference cut recall by more than two thirds, a verbal task hardly any.
numbers: Charness: 6-8% decrease with 30 s delay, but a longer latency for the first piece. Bradley et al: same pattern in tactical problems but the drop was about one third.
limits: Frey and Adesman (1976) used 8 s per board, which Gobet and Simon say the original theory can explain with 5 to 10 s learning time per chunk. Goldin (1978) deep-processing results are confounded with study time.
agent_relevance: The authors patched the model rather than dropping it. We should test patches, not accept them.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions (Memory & Cognition 24, 493-503): simulation
finding: A discrimination-net simulation (20 random fixations, equal to 5 s of human viewing) with nets up to 70,000 nodes reproduces human recall patterns. Recall rises with the log of the number of nodes, and mirror-reflected positions are recalled worse.
numbers: Normal 65.4% vs horizontal mirror 63.2% (F(1,13)=19.80, p<.005); vertical and central about 53.3% and 52.5%. The log function accounts for more than 98% of variance. Random positions rise only to 23.4%.
limits: Simulation only. It supports about 50,000 location-specific chunks against Holding's claim of about 2,500 location-free chunks.
agent_relevance: Cues tied to context beat context-free cues. Retrieval keys for the agent should include the situation, not only surface features.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions: human experiment 2
finding: Humans recalled normal and horizontally mirrored positions better than vertically or centrally mirrored ones at every skill level. This favours chunks that encode exact location.
numbers: N=25 (5 masters mean Elo 2395, 11 experts 2146, 9 Class A 1890). Normal plus horizontal: masters 77.3%, experts 49.7%, Class A 34.5%. Vertical plus central: 62.9%, 38.6%, 27.5%. Contrast F(1,22)=96.79, p<.001; skill x type F(2,22)=3.48, p<.05.
limits: Small groups. Masters still recalled much even when a pattern was moved, so some location-free knowledge exists.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: patterns do not transfer freely when moved. Cue matching needs context fit.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of rapidly presented random chess positions is a function of skill
finding: A review of chess experiments with random positions (3 to 10 s presentation) shows strong players keep a small advantage on random positions. The widely cited vanishing-expertise result is overstated.
numbers: Skill levels differ reliably on random positions in reviewed data, e.g. F(3,17)=10.35, p<.05 in one study. Relative difference far smaller than for game positions.
limits: Review of other labs' data. Effect sizes differ by study.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication note: the textbook claim that experts show no edge on random material is not safe. Do not build a gate on it.

source: Richman, Staszewski & Simon (1995) Simulation of expert memory using EPAM IV (Psychological Review 102, 305-330)
finding: EPAM IV adds a retrieval structure and an associative search in long-term memory. It reproduces earlier EPAM results and the digit-span expert DD. Chess templates are said to be programmed by Gobet on the same ideas.
numbers: Model fit to subject DD's recall of long digit sequences; fine-grained fit numbers not extracted.
limits: The digit-span fit is the main test. The chess part is cited, not tested here.
agent_relevance: A formal model exists for fast-store, slot-fill memory. Not directly an agent design.

source: Gobet (1997) A pattern-recognition theory of search in expert problem solving (Thinking & Reasoning 3, 291-313)
finding: The subfield key paper. As recalled from its abstract, not opened: templates may help search by storing information rapidly, by allowing search in template space as well as move space, and by making up for limited short-term memory.
numbers: No numbers recorded. Full text and abstract were not available this session (publisher page returned 403).
limits: From memory of the abstract only. Treat as unverified. Crossref confirms title, volume 3, pages 291-313, Nov 1997.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis: a cue library that supports search in the space of cues, not only in the space of moves.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess (NeurIPS 2024): searchless grandmaster play
finding: A transformer trained by supervised learning to predict Stockfish action values plays at grandmaster level with no search at test time. This is pattern recognition at scale.
numbers: Models of 9M, 136M and 270M parameters on 10M games (15.3B action values). 270M: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans, 2299 vs bots, 95.4% on 10K puzzles. Stockfish 16 (50 ms) 99.8%. Leela with 400 MCTS sims tournament Elo 2858 vs policy-only 2292 and value-only 2418. AlphaZero 400 sims 2470 vs policy-only 1777. Tournament Elo 270M 2299 (+-15), 9M 2025.
limits: Labels come from Stockfish (a search engine), so search is hidden in the labels. Elo drops against bots. Perfect distillation not reached. Tournament and Lichess Elo are not comparable. Under 1.41% of puzzle boards were in training.
agent_relevance: Recognition alone can reach high skill when the cue set is learned at huge scale. Search still adds roughly 400 to 700 Elo for Leela and AlphaZero.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024): scaling and the GPT-3.5 baseline
finding: Puzzle accuracy rose with model size and data size and did not come from memorisation. A general language model, GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct, scored far lower.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct: Lichess Elo vs bots 1755, puzzle accuracy 66.5%. 9M transformer 88.9%; 136M 94.5%. AlphaZero policy-only 56.1%, value-only 82.0%, 400 sims 95.6%.
limits: Training formats differ across systems (FEN vs PGN), so comparisons are rough.
agent_relevance: Language models without domain-specific cue training are weak; the cue library has to be built or learned for the domain.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of learned look-ahead in a chess-playing neural network
finding: Leela Chess Zero's policy network seems to represent moves two turns ahead inside its activations. A recognition-style network learns something like internal search.
numbers: A linear probe predicts the optimal move two turns ahead with 92% accuracy (puzzles where Leela finds a single best line). Probe trained on 70% of puzzles, tested on 30%. First and second move targets coincide in 83% of filtered puzzles vs 47% in the original set.
limits: Puzzle set was filtered to forced lines. Not shown for quiet positions. Existence proof, not a measure of compute saved.
agent_relevance: Boundary of the pattern-only view: fast networks may internalise search steps, so recognition and search may not separate cleanly.

source: McGrath et al. (2022) Acquisition of chess knowledge in AlphaZero (PNAS 2022)
finding: Human chess concepts (material, threats, king safety) become linearly decodable from AlphaZero's activations during training, with a rapid phase of change in concepts and in opening choices.
numbers: 1,000,000 training steps, batch 4096. Many concepts start rising near 32,000 steps. Stockfish 8 evaluation decodable only after about 16,000 steps and plateaus at 128,000. Piece values converge to accepted values after about 128,000 steps.
limits: Probes show information is present, not that it is used. Opening analysis is qualitative (Kramnik's comments).
agent_relevance: Learned recognisers come before good play. Supports building cheap feature detectors first, then search on top.

source: Schultz et al. (2024) Mastering board games by external and internal planning with language models
finding: A language model (MAV) trained as world model, value function and policy plays chess at grandmaster level. Adding MCTS or in-context minimax search adds strength, and Elo rises about logarithmically with test-time compute.
numbers: Searchless MAV external Elo 2923 (mean scoring) or 2875 (max scoring). MAV+MCTS with 100 simulations: internal Elo 68 above searchless MAV. In Connect Four all agents gained at least 244 Elo from MCTS. 14,689 chess tournament games. About 10% of positions played appear in the training set.
limits: Trained on engine-labelled data. Search budget is small compared with engines. Hex state tracking incomplete.
agent_relevance: Search on top of a recogniser gives smooth gains with compute: recognition first, then bounded search. Supports a search budget behind a cue gate.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models (COLM 2024)
finding: A GPT trained only on next-character prediction of chess game text builds an internal board state and also estimates player skill. Editing these variables changes play.
numbers: Legal move rate 99.8% (16 layers) and 99.6% (8 layers). Win rate vs Stockfish 16 level 0 (1300 Elo): 46% (8 layers), 64% (16 layers). Best board probe accuracy 99.6%. Skill intervention raised win rate 2x (8 layer) and 2.6x (16 layer). Elo probe called 99.4% of random-opening games low skill.
limits: Small model, human games, 1300-level engine only. Probes show representation, not necessarily use.
agent_relevance: Models track a latent skill level; a high-skill cue in context may lift play. Worth testing as a cheap S0 prompt cue.

source: Toshniwal et al. (2022) Chess as a testbed for language model state tracking (AAAI 2022)
finding: Transformers trained only on move strings can track piece positions and predict legal moves with high accuracy given enough data. Small data or approximate attention weakens this.
numbers: Piece-location accuracy 91.3% with the small training set vs perfect with the large one (UCI + RAP). Legal move accuracy above 97% for both UCI and UCI + RAP. Gap between exact piece moved and any piece of the same type above 8% absolute.
limits: Synthetic move notation, no search or skill evaluation. Measures state tracking, not move quality.
agent_relevance: State tracking is learnable but data-hungry; for an agent, re-reading state from the board each step is safer than trusting memory.

source: Competing accounts of recognition versus search in chess (Gobet & Simon 1996, 1998 summary)
finding: Three positions in the literature: recognition first (de Groot; Simon and Chase), search first (Holding 1985, SEEK), and a mix with recognition at each node (Gobet & Simon 1998). Evidence for each is indirect.
numbers: No single test splits them: Kasparov natural experiment (about 100 Elo lost), Calderwood blitz study (no big quality loss), Holding & Reynolds (skill correlated with search quality but not with random-position recall).
limits: Each test has confounds (preparation, subjective ratings, memory test at the root only).
agent_relevance: Do not treat one result as proof. Run our own ablation: cue gate on vs off at equal tokens (G7).
